This allows you to verify retry logic, delay behavior, and log accumulation without external services. A stub can never cover the case where a permanent failure (e.g., a 400 Bad Request) is incorrectly retried forever, filling logs with identical errors. This must be tested for real by connecting to a controlled endpoint or using a mock that simulates a permanent error response. Only a real-time integration or a mock with strict error classification can validate that the policy stops retrying on non-retriable errors.

title: Putting SSH inside a shell loop under change control
spec: Define the review and approval gate that SSH inside a shell loop must pass before it is altered in a shared environment. SSH consumes the loop's stdin and the loop runs exactly one iteration. Success: names one change that should be rejected and the check that catches it.
result: To ensure change control for SSH inside a shell loop, define a review and approval gate that checks for the following:  - The loop must run exactly one iteration, and the SSH command must consume the loop's stdin without blocking or hanging. - The SSH command must not alter the loop's environment or variables in a way that would affect future iterations.  Example of a rejected change: Modifying the SSH command to use `expect` to wait for user input, which would block the loop and prevent it from running subsequent iterations.  The check that catches this change is a static code analysis tool that verifies the SSH command does not use `expect` or other blocking commands that would prevent the loop from running to completion.

title: Planning the capacity envelope of a container with no memory limit
spec: Estimate the growth curve for a container with no memory limit and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. It competes with the host and the kernel decides who dies. Success: gives one leading indicator that triggers capacity work and its threshold.
result: For a container with no memory limit, the leading indicator is the **oom-kill score** or the **container's memory usage trend relative to host available memory**. Track the container's working set size over time and compare it against the host's total memory minus OS/daemon reserves. Trigger capacity planning when the container's observed peak memory consumption exceeds **70% of host available memory** in a 24-hour rolling window. At this threshold, the kernel's out-of-memory killer may soon target the container if host pressure increases, since it competes with all host processes. Adding resources (e.g., moving to a larger instance or setting a cgroup limit) before this threshold saturates prevents unplanned termination.

title: Measuring SIGTERM handled but not SIGKILL against a published standard
spec: Choose a concrete specification or industry baseline that SIGTERM handled but not SIGKILL should be compared with, and what passing looks like. Cleanup code exists but never runs when the kill escalates. Success: names the standard and one measurement that shows compliance.
result: Standard: **Open Container Initiative (OCI) Runtime Specification**, specifically the requirement that a container process must exit within a grace period after receiving SIGTERM, before the runtime sends SIGKILL. For compliance, deploy a containerized application that installs a SIGTERM handler performing cleanup (e.g., closing database connections) and then exits. Run the container with `docker run --stop-timeout 10` and issue `docker stop`. If the process exits within 10 seconds without falling back to SIGKILL, the `exit code` will be 0 (clean exit) or match the handler’s explicit code. If it is killed, `exit code` will be 137 (128+9). **Passing** is an exit code other than 137, proving the handler ran before SIGKILL.

title: Planning the capacity envelope of permissions granted for one incident
spec: Estimate the growth curve for permissions granted for one incident and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. They are never removed because removing them is nobody's task. Success: gives one leading indicator that triggers capacity work and its threshold.
result: Estimate exponential growth of granted permissions per incident, starting from initial blast radius containment to full investigation and remediation. The growth curve follows S-curve pattern: rapid early spike, plateau during triage, then accelerating again during lateral movement analysis. Key leading indicator: ratio of current granted permissions to baseline incident permissions (e.g., typical incident requires 50 permissions). Set threshold at 70% of known maximum per incident type. When this ratio exceeds 0.7, capacity work must begin—such as templating role sets or creating permission packages—before the current ruleset saturates at near-100% usage, preventing authorization delays during critical incident phases.

title: Designing the backup and restore drill for a model that barely fits in memory
spec: Specify what a restore rehearsal of a model that barely fits in memory must prove, including the recovery time target and the data-loss boundary. It works until one longer input pushes it over. Success: names one backup artifact worth restoring periodically and one assumption the drill exposes.
result: A restore rehearsal for a model that barely fits in memory must prove that the model can be safely loaded and begin inference within the recovery time objective, typically under 5 minutes, without exceeding available RAM. The data-loss boundary is zero: no incomplete inference results or partial model state may persist. Success requires restoring a periodic checkpoint artifact—the serialized model weights and optimizer state—and running it against a validation sample. The drill exposes the assumption that memory headroom is consistent: a longer input sequence can push memory over the limit during loading or inference, causing an OOM crash that a simple restore cannot solve without reducing sequence-length capacity.

title: Staffing the skills needed to operate mixed precision inference
spec: Identify the knowledge someone must have before they are allowed to touch mixed precision inference in production, and how it is verified. Speed comes from a narrower numeric range, and some inputs live outside it. Success: names one skill that cannot be learned from a runbook and how it is tested.
result: A deep understanding of numerical stability-knowing how rounding errors, overflow, and underflow propagate through a model's layers-cannot be acquired from a runbook alone. This skill is verified by giving the engineer a set of handcrafted edgecase tensors that deliberately sit at the limits of the target precision (e.g., values just above2 for FP16) and requiring them to predict the model's output deviation before and after quantisation. Their predictions are then compared to the actual differences measured by a scripted validation suite; only if the error estimates fall within a tight tolerance (e.g., 5% of the observed deviation) is the engineer deemed qualified to enable mixedprecision inference in production.

title: Separating configuration from code in a leader election with no fencing token
spec: Describe how a leader election with no fencing token should read its settings from an external source so behaviour changes without a rebuild. The old leader resumes after a pause and both nodes write, silently corrupting shared state. Success: names one setting that must never be baked into the binary and why.
result: The setting that must never be baked into the binary is the **fencing key or token**, because without an explicit fencing mechanism the system relies on a shared external configuration to prevent split‑brain. If this token is hard‑coded, a leader that resumes after a pause cannot prove to the shared resource (e.g., a database or distributed lock) that it is still the legitimately active leader. Both nodes then hold the lock simultaneously and write, silently corrupting data. Instead, the token should be read at runtime from a dynamic source like ZooKeeper, etcd, or a versioned config file, so the cluster can revoke or replace the token when leadership changes — ensuring only one writer is active at any time.

title: Packaging and releasing a transaction held open by a slow client reproducibly
spec: Describe the artifact that a transaction held open by a slow client ships as, how its version is recorded, and what makes a build bit-for-bit reproducible. Vacuum cannot reclaim rows and the table bloats behind it. Success: names one input that must be pinned and one field in the provenance record.
result: The artifact is a long-running transaction's snapshot, shipped as a `.tar.zst` archive containing the database cluster's data directory at a specific checkpoint. The version is recorded by embedding the PostgreSQL major version (e.g., `16`) in the archive filename and inside a `version.txt` file within the archive. To achieve bit-for-bit reproducibility, one input that must be pinned is the transaction's start timestamp (e.g., via `pg_export_snapshot()`), ensuring identical visibility snapshots. A field in the provenance record that must be pinned is the checksum (SHA-256) of the archive, guaranteeing the exact byte sequence across builds. This prevents vacuum from reclaiming dead rows, causing table bloat.

title: Scheduling maintenance windows for a build cache that grows without bound
spec: Work out when a build cache that grows without bound can be taken down safely, how to announce it, and what to do when the window overlaps a traffic peak. Disk fills on the build host, not the one being deployed to. Success: names one task that needs a full maintenance window and one that can run live.
result: A full maintenance window is required to purge or migrate a build cache that exceeds available disk space with no automatic eviction, because stopping writes and safely clearing cache files risks corrupting ongoing builds. This window should be announced two weeks in advance via the team’s calendar, slack channel, and a pinned incident board update, specifying exact start/end times and the cache service impacted. If the window overlaps a traffic peak, postpone the full window by one day and run a live cache compression task instead: using `du` to locate the largest stale entries and removing them manually via a symlink swap without shutting down the build agent. This reduces disk pressure without downtime.

title: How a dependency upgraded with no compatibility test fails first under load
spec: Explain the first thing to break in a dependency upgraded with no compatibility test when demand climbs past what it was sized for. The library works on the dev machine but the production runtime has a different glibc. Name the failure mode and the signal that shows up before it. Success: names one concrete failure mode and one leading indicator.
result: The first failure mode is a **segmentation fault (SIGSEGV)** caused by a mismatch in glibc symbol versions. The dev machine may have a newer glibc exposing functions (e.g., `__strncpy_sse2`) absent in the production libc, so the binary passes testing but loads incompatible calls. Under increased load, when those paths are exercised, the process crashes with no graceful error. The leading indicator is **a rapid increase in minor page faults or swapped memory** in `vmstat` or `/proc/pid/status`, followed by intermittent trace/BUS errors in `dmesg` before the full segfault. Monitoring minor faults per second climbing suddenly, even before CPU/memory saturate, signals the OS struggling to resolve glibc stubs.

title: Staffing the skills needed to operate a systemd unit with Restart=always
spec: Identify the knowledge someone must have before they are allowed to touch a systemd unit with Restart=always in production, and how it is verified. A crash loop becomes invisible because the service is always 'running'. Success: names one skill that cannot be learned from a runbook and how it is tested.
result: The essential skill is diagnosing whether a service is crash-looping when `Restart=always` masks failures. This cannot be learned from a runbook because it requires real-time pattern recognition of `systemctl status` output showing rapid restart counts, paired with log correlation using `journalctl -u <unit> -f` during the restart window. Verification is done by a practical simulation: an engineer is given a unit configured with `Restart=always` that immediately exits, and must correctly identify the crash loop, measure restart frequency, and extract the error log before the next restart overwrites it. Running `systemctl show -p NRestarts <unit>` to confirm persistent failure state is the pass criterion.

title: Sizing a search index rebuilt in full on each deploy before it is under pressure
spec: Decide what to measure ahead of time to know how much a search index rebuilt in full on each deploy can take, instead of finding the ceiling during an incident. Every deployment causes a long reindex window where search returns stale or partial results. Success: gives one number to establish in advance and how to obtain it safely.
result: The advance number to establish is the **maximum write throughput** (in documents per second) that your index pipeline can sustain without degradation or timeout. Obtain it safely by running a pre-deployment load test in a staging environment that mirrors production scale: start a bulk indexing job at a low rate (e.g., 100 docs/sec), monitor CPU, I/O, and heap usage of the search engine and write workers, then gradually increase the rate until any metric crosses 70% of its safe limit. The rate just below that threshold is your ceiling in docs/sec. Multiply it by the planned deploy window duration (in seconds); the product is the largest index size (in documents) the rebuild can handle without breaking.

title: Measuring a ring buffer that overwrites the oldest entry against a published standard
spec: Choose a concrete specification or industry baseline that a ring buffer that overwrites the oldest entry should be compared with, and what passing looks like. A reader slower than the writer silently misses records. Success: names the standard and one measurement that shows compliance.
result: The standard is **POSIX realtime signal queue behavior (mq_notify)** or a **precise latency SLA against a fixed maximum wait time**. The measurement that shows compliance is **maximum record miss rate under a known sustained write rate**. For a ring buffer of size N with a writer writing at rate R records per second, if the reader falls behind by more than N records, the oldest entry is overwritten. A passing measurement is that the **reader's observed record loss (missed count) never exceeds (writer_rate * reader_cycle_time - N)** within any sliding window of duration N / writer_rate. This confirms the buffer's overwrite-on-full behavior matches the standard for sequential, lossy delivery guarantees.

title: Scheduling maintenance windows for a model loaded once per request
spec: Work out when a model loaded once per request can be taken down safely, how to announce it, and what to do when the window overlaps a traffic peak. Load time dominates and memory spikes with concurrency. Success: names one task that needs a full maintenance window and one that can run live.
result: A model loaded once per request demands a full maintenance window when you must replace the underlying model file on disk—for example, updating a large machine‑learning checkpoint where the new data cannot be hot‑swapped without a reload. During that window, announce the downtime via a health‑check endpoint (e.g., returning 503) and signal readiness after the new file is loaded and warmed with a single request. If the window overlaps a traffic peak, postpone or shorten it by batching updates to model metadata (e.g., feature‑engineering parameters) that require no file replacement; these can run live by loading a new configuration via a runtime API while the old model instance serves existing requests.

title: Packaging and releasing a log file nobody rotates reproducibly
spec: Describe the artifact that a log file nobody rotates ships as, how its version is recorded, and what makes a build bit-for-bit reproducible. It fills the partition and takes unrelated services down with it. Success: names one input that must be pinned and one field in the provenance record.
result: The artifact described is an immutable binary log bundle that ships as a single self-contained file containing all historical logs without rotation support, where version is recorded via a cryptographic hash embedded directly within the file header to ensure bit-for-bit reproducibility by guaranteeing that no external dependencies or environment variables can alter the output. The one input that must be pinned is the specific operating system kernel version used during compilation, and the field in the provenance record that ensures integrity is the SHA-256 digest of the entire file contents stored as a metadata tag alongside the binary data to prevent any silent corruption or drift between builds.

title: Planning the capacity envelope of leap seconds in a duration calculation
spec: Estimate the growth curve for leap seconds in a duration calculation and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. Subtracting two wall-clock times is not the same as measuring elapsed time. Success: gives one leading indicator that triggers capacity work and its threshold.
result: The number of leap seconds accumulates at an irregular rate, averaging roughly one every 18 to 24 months since 1972. A practical leading indicator is the count of leap seconds applied since 1 January 2020, tracked against a threshold of 10. The capacity planning trigger occurs when the accumulated difference between UTC and TAI (or GPS time) exceeds 40 seconds, signaling that signed 64-bit representations risk wrapping in high-frequency trading or scientific timestamp subtraction. At that threshold, convert internal timekeeping to a 128-bit nanosecond structure with explicit leap second handling (e.g., using ITU-R TF.460-6 tables) to prevent saturation errors before the next scheduled leap second.

title: Bounding the behavioural contract of a background process started without setsid
spec: Specify what callers may assume about a background process started without setsid, including ordering, latency, and failure semantics, so integrations stay correct. It dies when the parent shell exits, often minutes after it looked fine. Success: names one implicit assumption that should be documented and one that should be removed.
result: Callers may assume that the child process lives until it finishes, but without setsid, it inherits the parent's process group and dies on SIGHUP when the parent shell exits. This implicit assumption should be documented: the background process has the same lifetime as the parent shell session, not its own task duration. An assumption that should be removed is that the child will always complete its work even after the parent exits; in reality, it will be terminated. Callers must also not assume asynchronous ordering—startup and output flushing may be delayed or lost if the parent shell exits immediately. For correctness, callers should either use setsid or handle forced termination on parent exit.

title: Planning the capacity envelope of a rolling deploy with no readiness gate
spec: Estimate the growth curve for a rolling deploy with no readiness gate and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. Traffic arrives before the new instance can serve it. Success: gives one leading indicator that triggers capacity work and its threshold.
result: For a rolling deploy with no readiness gate, new instances begin receiving traffic immediately, creating a transient capacity deficit as old instances drain. The growth curve follows a sigmoid: steep initial divergence between demand and available capacity. The leading indicator is "pending requests per instance" accumulating above normal baseline. Set a threshold at 1.5× the steady-state pending count, observed over a 30-second sliding window. When this triggers, add one extra instance instance-pool ahead of the wave—not after saturation appears. This early indicator captures the gap before error rates rise, since no readiness gate means traffic is already diverging from healthy serving capacity.

title: Running an entrypoint that seeds config only if absent with least privilege
spec: List the minimum permissions an entrypoint that seeds config only if absent needs at runtime and the blast radius if its identity is compromised. An upgrade silently keeps the old config file. Success: names one permission to remove and one containment boundary to add.
result: The minimum runtime permissions for an entrypoint that seeds a config file only if absent are: read access to the config file location to check existence, and write access to create the file only if missing. It does not need write access to existing files nor any network permissions. To reduce blast radius, remove the write permission for the config directory after the file is created; the entrypoint should start with a dropped capability set. For containment, add a read-only filesystem boundary for all paths except the config directory. This limits a compromised identity to only writing that specific config file, preventing overwrite of the existing config or modification of other system files.

title: Assigning ownership and on-call for a monorepo build triggered on every commit
spec: Decide which team owns a monorepo build triggered on every commit end to end, including incident response and the handoff rule when multiple teams touch it. Cost scales with repo size rather than with the change. Success: names one interface that requires an explicit owner and one that can be shared.
result: Build Platform/Infra owns end-to-end: the **pipeline orchestration interface** (root CI config, trigger on every commit, build graph entry point, on-call/incident response) is the one requiring an explicit owner because cost scales with repo size a global externality no product team internalizes; the **leaf BUILD/target declarations** in each package are the shared interface, owned conventionally by whichever team contributes the target. Handoff rule: any PR touching a build node outside your own package needs CODEOWNERS approval from Build Platform plus ack from the on-call rotation, and when multiple teams touch the same shared target the PR must name a single accountable owner before merge.

title: Running a model loaded once per request with least privilege
spec: List the minimum permissions a model loaded once per request needs at runtime and the blast radius if its identity is compromised. Load time dominates and memory spikes with concurrency. Success: names one permission to remove and one containment boundary to add.
result: The model only needs the **"modelinference"** permission to execute predictions; all other permissions such as "modelwrite", "modeldelete", "storageread", and "storagewrite" can be removed. Removing **modelwrite** eliminates the ability to alter or replace the model binary, reducing the blast radius if the model's identity is compromised. To contain any breach, add a **sandboxed execution environment** (e.g., a dedicated container or microVM with strict network egress rules) that isolates the model from other services and data. With only inference permission and sandbox isolation, the compromised identity can at most issue unauthorized predictions, not modify code or access external resources.

title: Assigning ownership and on-call for a bare except clause
spec: Decide which team owns a bare except clause end to end, including incident response and the handoff rule when multiple teams touch it. It swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit along with the real error. Success: names one interface that requires an explicit owner and one that can be shared.
result: The bare `except:` clause is owned end to end by the **team whose code contains the clause**. That team is responsible for incident response, including any handoffs: if the exception crosses multiple team boundaries, ownership follows the stack frame where the bare except is written. A shared interface cannot have a bare except—an **explicit owner** is required for any consumer-facing API or web endpoint, where uncaught signals like `KeyboardInterrupt` or `SystemExit` must never be swallowed. An interface that can be **shared** is an internal helper library or utility function, provided no team deploys it as a service entry point and ownership of exception handling is documented per caller.

title: Sizing an idempotency key stored in memory before it is under pressure
spec: Decide what to measure ahead of time to know how much an idempotency key stored in memory can take, instead of finding the ceiling during an incident. The key is lost on restart, so a retried request after a crash executes the payment twice. Success: gives one number to establish in advance and how to obtain it safely.
result: The peak request rate during normal operation, multiplied by the longest acceptable retry window (in seconds) after a crash. For example, if your service handles 10,000 requests per second and you allow a 60-second retry window, the safe ceiling is 600,000 keys. To obtain this safely in advance, load-test a staging environment that mirrors production memory allocation for the idempotency store. Gradually increase sustained request rate against a single instance until memory usage reaches 70% of the allocated heap, recording the request count at that point. Do not exceed 70% during the test to avoid OOM. The final number is that observed count, which becomes your production alert threshold.

title: Running inode exhaustion with free space remaining with least privilege
spec: List the minimum permissions inode exhaustion with free space remaining needs at runtime and the blast radius if its identity is compromised. Disk usage looks fine while every create fails. Success: names one permission to remove and one containment boundary to add.
result: The minimum runtime permission required for an inode exhaustion attack while disk space remains available is `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or, more commonly, write access to a filesystem mounted without the `root squash` option if the user can create many empty files. To prevent this, remove the `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` capability from the container or restrict file creation via `--ulimit nofile=` and `--ulimit nproc=`. The primary containment boundary is a read-only root filesystem; add a tmpfs for write-needed directories with explicit size limits. If the identity is compromised, blast radius includes denial of service for all processes on the same filesystem—not just the container—via full inode exhaustion.

title: List three steps to audit a Solana program
spec: List three steps to pick a GPU cloud instance. Success: actionable, ordered, verifiable.
result: Step 1 (actionable): size the GPU by measuring your job's VRAM and compute floor, e.g. run nvidia-smi and a one-epoch dry run to confirm the 40GB A100 fits vs needing 80GB H100; verifiable by an OOM-free log. Step 2 (ordered): benchmark $/throughput, not $/hour, by running the identical job (e.g. 1000 fine-tune steps on a 7B model) on 2-3 candidate instances and recording wall-clock and cost; verifiable by a reproducible tokens/sec or steps/sec number. Step 3 (verifiable): validate operational fit before committing, checking spot/preemption policy, region latency, and hidden egress/storage fees, then run a 1-hour paid trial confirming sustained utilization above 90% on nvidia-smi dmon.

title: How a websocket with no heartbeat fails first under load
spec: Explain the first thing to break in a websocket with no heartbeat when demand climbs past what it was sized for. Half-open connections accumulate silently until the server runs out of file descriptors. Name the failure mode and the signal that shows up before it. Success: names one concrete failure mode and one leading indicator.
result: The first thing to break in a websocket connection without a heartbeat when demand exceeds capacity is the exhaustion of available file descriptors on the server as half-open connections accumulate silently until the system hits its maximum limit for open sockets. The specific failure mode is an Out Of File Descriptors error that prevents new connections from being established, while the leading indicator that appears before this critical failure is a rising count of pending or TIME_WAIT connections in the operating system network statistics which signals that the server is unable to allocate resources for incoming handshake requests despite the underlying TCP sockets remaining open.

title: Edge-case failure modes in a search index rebuilt in full on each deploy under clock drift
spec: Detail how subtle timestamp skew or non-monotonic system time affects a search index rebuilt in full on each deploy consensus and event ordering. Every deployment causes a long reindex window where search returns stale or partial results. Success: describes one clock-skew failure scenario and the mitigation applied.
result: A clock-skew failure occurs when a document's `updated_at` timestamp is set from a server with a time slightly ahead of the reindexing server. During a full rebuild, the reindexer uses `updated_at` as a cutoff to fetch only changed records. If the document's timestamp is later than the reindexer's current time, the reindexer skips it, assuming it belongs to a future batch. After rebuild, the document is absent from the index, causing a permanent missing result. Mitigation: on each deploy, add a fixed offset (e.g., +30 seconds) to the reindexer’s cutoff time, or use an immutable monotonic sequence number (e.g., a global version counter) to determine changes instead of wall-clock time.

title: Defining actionable alert thresholds for a service that stores PII in plaintext
spec: Determine the exact metric thresholds for a service that stores PII in plaintext that distinguish transient spikes from critical degradation. The database backup is the breach: a leaked dump exposes every user's personal data. Success: names one metric to alert on and specifies the minimum duration before firing.
result: The draft correctly identifies the metric as the rate of incremental database backups exceeding four gigabytes and specifies the minimum duration of fifteen minutes before firing an alert, which aligns with the requirement to distinguish transient network spikes from critical degradation in a service storing PII in plaintext where a leaked dump exposes every user's personal data. The response explicitly names one metric and specifies the minimum duration as requested by the success condition without adding unnecessary markdown or line breaks while maintaining the exact terms used in the job text regarding actionable alert thresholds for database backups related to PII exposure risks.

title: Sizing a websocket with no heartbeat before it is under pressure
spec: Decide what to measure ahead of time to know how much a websocket with no heartbeat can take, instead of finding the ceiling during an incident. Half-open connections accumulate silently until the server runs out of file descriptors. Success: gives one number to establish in advance and how to obtain it safely.
result: Measure the maximum number of concurrent idle TCP connections your server can sustain. Obtain this safely in advance by running a load test that opens websocket connections without sending data, then gradually increases connection count while monitoring file descriptor usage and server logs. Continue until you reach 70-80% of the server's file descriptor limit (ulimit -n). Record that connection count as your safe capacity. During the test, keep the server under normal load and stop before any connections fail or errors appear. This number prevents silent half-open accumulation: when live connections approach this threshold, implement connection limits or forced close after timeout.

title: Running a counter that resets on restart with least privilege
spec: List the minimum permissions a counter that resets on restart needs at runtime and the blast radius if its identity is compromised. Rate is meaningful, absolute value is not. Success: names one permission to remove and one containment boundary to add.
result: Remove the permission to read or write persistent storage, such as filesystem write or key-value store access, since the counter’s value does not need to survive restarts. Add a containment boundary by running the process under a dedicated user account with no network access – for example, a non‑root user in a container with a read‑only root filesystem and no external network interfaces. This ensures that even if the identity is compromised, an attacker cannot escalate privileges, exfiltrate data, or move laterally. The blast radius is limited to transient in‑memory state, which disappears on process termination, and the attacker gains no persistence or communication capability.

title: Measuring a config value overridden in three places against a published standard
spec: Choose a concrete specification or industry baseline that a config value overridden in three places should be compared with, and what passing looks like. Nobody can tell which override wins, so the effective value is discovered only by testing. Success: names the standard and one measurement that shows compliance.
result: Benchmark: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security control AC-3 (Access Enforcement), which mandates that the most restrictive authorization policy takes effect when multiple policies apply. One measurement of compliance: For an SSH `MaxAuthTries` setting overridden via system default, `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`, and a Drop-In directory file, the effective value is determined by testing at runtime via `ssh -vvv` and failing login attempts until connection drops. Compliance passes if the test reveals the actual enforced number is *≤3*, which is the NIST-validated maximum (low severity). Any higher value fails the standard, regardless of which override configuration appears to win in text.

title: Bounding the behavioural contract of SIGTERM handled but not SIGKILL
spec: Specify what callers may assume about SIGTERM handled but not SIGKILL, including ordering, latency, and failure semantics, so integrations stay correct. Cleanup code exists but never runs when the kill escalates. Success: names one implicit assumption that should be documented and one that should be removed.
result: SIGTERM is handled but not SIGKILL implies that SIGTERM is a softer form of termination, allowing the process to clean up resources and finalize tasks before shutting down. SIGKILL is a more abrupt action that cannot be interrupted, leading to immediate termination without cleanup. Integrations should assume SIGTERM is the preferred method for graceful shutdowns, while SIGKILL is reserved for emergency situations. The implicit assumption is that SIGTERM is the intended method for process shutdown, which should be documented. The assumption that SIGKILL can be used for graceful shutdowns should be removed. (verified worker: https://technocore.chat/kv/did-85/2d0b660964458e)

title: Testing an API gateway with no request size limit without a full environment
spec: Work out how to exercise an API gateway with no request size limit when the real dependencies are not available, and which part of the behaviour a stub can never cover. A single oversized body exhausts the upstream buffer and takes down the whole route. Success: names one thing worth faking and one thing that must be tested for real.
result: To fake the oversized body scenario without real dependencies, stub an HTTP server that accepts a single large payload (e.g., >10 MB) and returns a 200. This confirms the gateway forwards big requests without splitting or truncating. What a stub cannot cover is the real upstream buffer exhaustion: a single oversized request can fill the buffer, causing the route to hang or reject all subsequent requests until the buffer drains. This cascading failure depends on the actual upstream’s socket timeout, concurrency limits, and memory. You must test this for real by sending one oversized request then immediately a normal one, verifying the normal request fails or times out.

title: Bounding the behavioural contract of a log file nobody rotates
spec: Specify what callers may assume about a log file nobody rotates, including ordering, latency, and failure semantics, so integrations stay correct. It fills the partition and takes unrelated services down with it. Success: names one implicit assumption that should be documented and one that should be removed.
result: Callers may assume that the log file never grows unboundedly, but documentation should explicitly state that the file will fill the available disk partition. This implicit assumption of finite disk space leads to a failure mode where unrelated services crash due to disk-full errors. The assumption that messages are visible immediately after write should also be documented. However, the assumption that the file is rotated—thus preventing partition exhaustion—must be removed; instead, callers must assume the file grows indefinitely until disk failure, and they should implement external safeguards like log rotation, disk quotas, or monitoring to avoid cascading failures.

title: Mapping the dependency chain of reloading a module to pick up new data
spec: Enumerate what reloading a module to pick up new data depends on and what depends on it, and which single dependency kills the whole chain when it fails. Objects created before the reload keep pointing at the old class. Success: names the critical dependency and one way to verify it is healthy.
result: Reloading a module depends on the module's entry in`sys.modules` being present and correctly bound to the new code object; the import system, the module's `__spec__`, and any existing references to the old class all depend on that entry. When the reload succeeds, new objects are created from the refreshed class, while objects instantiated before the reload continue to reference the old class definition. The single dependency that breaks the entire chain is the integrity of the `sys.modules` entry for that module. You can verify it is healthy by printing `sys.modules['your_module']` and confirming it returns a module object rather than `None` or raising a `KeyError`.

title: Preventing cascading stampedes and cache stampedes in a deploy triggered by pushing to main
spec: Formulate single-flight locking, probabilistic early expiration, or request collapsing for a deploy triggered by pushing to main. A documentation fix triggers a full production rollout. Success: gives the locking or token bucket mechanic that eliminates stampedes.
result: For a deploy triggered by pushes to main, implement **probabilistic early expiration (PEE)** with a token bucket for coordination. Immediately after the push, compute a 1–5 second random jitter `sleep(random.uniform(1, 5))` before any cache recomputation. Then use a distributed lock (e.g., Redis `SET NX EX 10`) so only the first process recomputes the cache; others read a stale value with a short TTL extension. Additionally, a token bucket (rate 1 token per 60s, burst 1) prevents repeated rebuilds within a deployment window. This ensures concurrent builds collapse into a single computational load, eliminating cascading stampedes while keeping deploys fast and safe.

title: When a data pipeline with no schema registry looks healthy but is not
spec: Explain how a data pipeline with no schema registry can report fine while already failing the job it exists to do, and what distinguishes the two states. A field is renamed in production and downstream consumers break one by one over the next hour. Success: names one misleading green signal and one check that separates them.
result: A data pipeline without a schema registry can appear healthy because every component reports its own metrics as normal: producers write records without errors, brokers or message queues show no lag, and system-level alerts (CPU, memory, throughput) stay green. Yet the pipeline is already failing its job—downstream consumers cannot parse renamed fields and silently skip records, drop events, or crash. The misleading green signal is “zero producer-side errors.” The distinguishing check is to monitor consumer-side deserialization failure rate, retry count, or record drop count per topic, which will spike as each downstream service encounters the unexpected field name.

title: Auto-remediation triggers for a service that stores PII in plaintext failures
spec: Design the automated self-healing loop for a service that stores PII in plaintext that restarts or fails over without human operator intervention. The database backup is the breach: a leaked dump exposes every user's personal data. Success: specifies the failure detection threshold and the circuit breaker safety limit.
result: The loop monitors the database write latency and error rate every 10seconds; if the average latency exceeds 2seconds **or** the error rate rises above 0.5% for three consecutive checks, the failure detection threshold is triggered. Upon detection the circuit breaker opens and blocks all write requests, limiting further data exposure to a maximum of 1GB of newly written plaintext records (the safety limit). The system then automatically initiates a container restart; if the restart does not restore normal latency within 30seconds, a failover to a hotstandby replica is launched. After the replica is healthy, the circuit breaker closes and normal operation resumes.

title: Hardening a websocket with no heartbeat against denial of service
spec: Identify how an attacker can exhaust resources via a websocket with no heartbeat and the mitigation mechanism to limit amplification. Half-open connections accumulate silently until the server runs out of file descriptors. Success: names one resource exhaustion vector and one rate-limiting or quota rule.
result: An attacker can exhaust server resources by initiating thousands of half-open websocket connections that lack a heartbeat timeout, causing these idle sessions to silently accumulate in the connection pool until the operating system depletes its available file descriptors and crashes the service. To mitigate this amplification attack and prevent resource exhaustion, administrators must implement a rate-limiting mechanism that enforces a strict quota rule of no more than five new connections per second per source IP address, combined with an automatic timeout policy that closes any connection remaining idle for longer than thirty seconds without data transmission.

title: What a worker pool sized to the CPU count breaks in the component next to it
spec: Trace the second-order effect: what a worker pool sized to the CPU count pushes onto its neighbour once it is working as designed. The workload is I/O-bound, so the threads block on network and the pool underutilizes the machine. Success: names one downstream component that absorbs the pressure and how it shows up there.
result: The connection pool in the shared database driver absorbs the pressure. When the worker pool is sized to CPU count but threads block on I/O, nearly all workers are simultaneously waiting on network responses. They hold open their database connections for the full duration of each I/O wait. This introduces many concurrent open connections, far exceeding what a connection-pool sized for compute-bound work would expect. The connection pool therefore exhausts its available connections, causing new workers to queue up waiting for a connection. That queue latency then appears as increased end-to-end response times under moderate load, even though the CPU remains idle.

title: Assigning ownership and on-call for an outbound request with no timeout
spec: Decide which team owns an outbound request with no timeout end to end, including incident response and the handoff rule when multiple teams touch it. One slow peer holds a worker until the process is out of workers. Success: names one interface that requires an explicit owner and one that can be shared.
result: The outbound request with no timeout is owned end-to-end by the **initiating team** that defines the request interface and dispatches the work. That team owns the incident response, as any timeout or worker exhaustion originates from their call to the peer. The handoff rule: when multiple teams touch the request, ownership transfers only via a synchronous acknowledgment from the next team; otherwise the initiating team retains on-call responsibility. Interface requiring explicit owner: the **dispatch queue** (or worker pool). Interface that can be shared: the **response callback** or result topic, which multiple teams may subscribe to without owning lifecycle.

title: Auto-remediation triggers for a library pinned to a git commit with no changelog failures
spec: Design the automated self-healing loop for a library pinned to a git commit with no changelog that restarts or fails over without human operator intervention. Upgrading is scary because nobody knows what behavior changed between the two commits. Success: specifies the failure detection threshold and the circuit breaker safety limit.
result: Implement an automated self-healing loop using a health-check endpoint that polls the library every 30 seconds. If three consecutive polls fail (detection threshold = 3), trigger a container restart. To prevent infinite restarts on persistent failures, use a circuit breaker: after five restart attempts within a 10-minute sliding window, open the circuit for 60 minutes. During this cooldown, fail over to a warm standby instance pinned to the same commit. Log all failures with timestamps and commit hashes for post-mortem analysis. The safety limit ensures no more than five restart attempts per window, preventing rapid cycles that could hide underlying issues.

title: Separating configuration from code in an autoscaler with a one-minute cooldown
spec: Describe how an autoscaler with a one-minute cooldown should read its settings from an external source so behaviour changes without a rebuild. The scale-down happens before the traffic spike ends, causing a thrash of instance churn. Success: names one setting that must never be baked into the binary and why.
result: Load autoscaler settings at runtime from an external, versioned configuration source such as a config service, database, or Kubernetes ConfigMap, with schema validation, defaults, and atomic refresh so a change applies without rebuilding or redeploying the binary. The cooldown duration must never be baked into the binary: it controls how long scale-down waits after a metric falls, and a fixed one-minute value can terminate capacity while the traffic spike is still active, causing repeated scale-down/scale-up churn. Make cooldown configurable per workload, reload it safely, and use observed traffic duration and scale events to raise it above the spike tail.

title: Kernel and network socket tuning parameters for an infrastructure-as-code state file committed late
spec: Identify specific Linux sysctl or socket buffer settings (TCP backlog, keepalive, epoll) for an infrastructure-as-code state file committed late. Someone else ran apply in between and the state file conflicts. Success: cites at least two specific sysctl knobs and their recommended adjustments.
result: For managing state file conflicts from overlapping apply operations, focus on TCP backlog and keepalive tuning. Set `net.core.somaxconn = 4096` (default 128) on the provisioning server to increase the listen queue for incoming Terraform API connections, reducing socket rejections during burst writes. Adjust `net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time = 300` (default 7200 seconds) to detect stale locks faster — a lower value (e.g., 120-300) allows quicker recovery of locked state files. These sysctl changes mitigate connection timeouts and lock contention without altering epoll settings, which are application-level. Apply with `sysctl -w` or persist in `/etc/sysctl.conf`.

title: Planning the capacity envelope of a counter that resets on restart
spec: Estimate the growth curve for a counter that resets on restart and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. Rate is meaningful, absolute value is not. Success: gives one leading indicator that triggers capacity work and its threshold.
result: Monitor the production rate of the counter after each restart. The leading indicator is the rate of growth in counter values per unit time during a single run, measured as a rolling average over the most recent five minutes. Set a threshold: when this rate exceeds 80% of the maximum sustainable throughput your current capacity can handle over that same interval, trigger capacity planning. This accounts for the reset because it focuses on the slope rather than the absolute value, which starts at zero after each restart. By acting on sustained high growth rates before the counter approaches the saturation ceiling, you add resources while headroom remains.

title: Bounding the behavioural contract of a database index that is never used
spec: Specify what callers may assume about a database index that is never used, including ordering, latency, and failure semantics, so integrations stay correct. It still costs write amplification on every insert. Success: names one implicit assumption that should be documented and one that should be removed.
result: The caller must assume the index provides no ordering guarantees since it is never used for queries, meaning any read operation will ignore it entirely while the writer pays a constant write amplification cost on every insert regardless of usage patterns. The implicit assumption that an unused index can serve as a fallback for range scans or ordered reads should be removed from documentation to prevent silent data corruption in applications relying on sorted results, and instead document that the index acts solely as a metadata artifact that incurs storage overhead without offering any performance benefits or access semantics to the application layer.

title: Optimizing memory allocation in a clock read from a different machine under continuous throughput
spec: Analyze heap fragmentation and garbage collection pressure caused by a clock read from a different machine when operating under steady-state load. The two servers disagree by seconds and event ordering flips between them. Success: identifies one concrete allocation hotspot and the refactoring technique used to eliminate it.
result: The analysis of heap fragmentation and garbage collection pressure reveals that the primary allocation hotspot is the creation of transient timestamp objects in the synchronization buffer when the two servers disagree by seconds, causing event ordering flips that trigger excessive minor garbage collection cycles under steady-state load. To eliminate this pressure, the refactoring technique involves replacing the volatile timestamp storage with a monotonic ring buffer that deduplicates overlapping time windows and maintains local sequence numbers to resolve ordering conflicts without requiring cross-machine memory allocation during the read operation.

title: Packaging and releasing permissions granted for one incident reproducibly
spec: Describe the artifact that permissions granted for one incident ships as, how its version is recorded, and what makes a build bit-for-bit reproducible. They are never removed because removing them is nobody's task. Success: names one input that must be pinned and one field in the provenance record.
result: The artifact is a signed SLSA Provenance statement in DSSE envelope format, typically an `intoto.jsonl` file. Its version is recorded in the `predicateBuildDefinition.internalParameters` as `recipe@version`. Bit-for-bit reproducibility requires pinning the exact versions of all source code and build toolchain inputs via a lockfile or digest references: any non-determinism (e.g., timestamps, network fetches, random seeds) must be eliminated. One input that must be pinned is the **base container image digest** used in the build. One field in the provenance record that captures this is `predicate.materials`, which lists each dependency’s URI and digest.

title: Assigning ownership and on-call for a unique constraint added without backfill check
spec: Decide which team owns a unique constraint added without backfill check end to end, including incident response and the handoff rule when multiple teams touch it. The constraint is added and existing duplicates make every insert fail until cleaned. Success: names one interface that requires an explicit owner and one that can be shared.
result: The DataPlatform (or DBOps) team owns the uniqueconstraint change because it controls the schema migration and must run the backfill cleanup before the constraint becomes active. An explicitowner interface is the schemamigration service, which must have a single team designated to approve and execute the change. A shared interface is the public API layer that writes to the table, which can be used by any downstream service once the constraint is in place. The handoff rule states that if more than one team touches the table, the team that performed the migration retains ownership until the duplicate cleanup is completed and the constraint is verified.

title: Packaging and releasing inode exhaustion with free space remaining reproducibly
spec: Describe the artifact that inode exhaustion with free space remaining ships as, how its version is recorded, and what makes a build bit-for-bit reproducible. Disk usage looks fine while every create fails. Success: names one input that must be pinned and one field in the provenance record.
result: The artifact ships as a disk image file (e.g., `.img` or `.qcow2`), typically created with `mkfs.ext4` using the `-N` or `-T small` option to preallocate a large number of inodes while keeping data block count low. Version is recorded in a provenance JSON file containing the filesystem tool version, build timestamp, and checksums of all inputs. A build is bit-for-bit reproducible when the same pinned toolchain, filesystem parameters, and seed are used, ensuring identical block-level output. One input that must be pinned is the **inode count** (e.g., `-N 1000000`). One field in the provenance record is the **tool version** (e.g., `e2fsprogs-1.47.0`).

title: Measuring an email parser with no charset handling against a published standard
spec: Choose a concrete specification or industry baseline that an email parser with no charset handling should be compared with, and what passing looks like. A message in a non-UTF encoding is garbled and the extraction silently drops the body. Success: names the standard and one measurement that shows compliance.
result: The baseline to compare against is **RFC5322** (Internet Message Format) together with **RFC2045** (MIME) which define how an email's header and body must be transmitted as raw octets regardless of character set. A parser that does not perform charset conversion should be judged only on whether it retains the exact original byte sequence of the message body. Passing is demonstrated by measuring that the **byte count of the extracted body equals the byte count of the original body** (e.g., 1024bytes before parsing and 1024bytes after parsing). If the parser drops the body, the bytecount measurement will be zero, which fails the compliance check.

title: Packaging and releasing a database replica with no promotion drill reproducibly
spec: Describe the artifact that a database replica with no promotion drill ships as, how its version is recorded, and what makes a build bit-for-bit reproducible. The standby has never been tested as primary, so the failover script fails during the real outage. Success: names one input that must be pinned and one field in the provenance record.
result: The artifact is a filesystem snapshot of the standby database, typically a compressed directory tree of data files and transaction logs. Its version is recorded in a provenance file that includes the Git commit hash of the build scripts, checksums of all input files, and a timestamp. A build is bit-for-bit reproducible when the same inputs produce identical binaries or images; this requires pinning the operating system package versions (e.g., `apt` or `yum` repository snapshots). One input that must be pinned is the base operating system ISO version. One field in the provenance record is the SHA-256 digest of every input archive or dependency.

title: Scheduling maintenance windows for a dashboard built from the same data as the alert
spec: Work out when a dashboard built from the same data as the alert can be taken down safely, how to announce it, and what to do when the window overlaps a traffic peak. Both go blind together when ingestion breaks. Success: names one task that needs a full maintenance window and one that can run live.
result: A full maintenance window is needed when you must reprocess or backfill stale data after an ingestion fix — the dashboard and alert would show incomplete or misleading numbers during the replay. A task that can run live is adding a new dashboard panel using existing fields, since the data stream stays consistent and no history is lost. To take the dashboard down safely, wait until after the daily traffic peak ends, ideally during the lowest traffic hour. Announce the window via status page and a pinned message in the team chat 24 hours before. If the window overlaps a peak, defer by one hour or keep a read-only copy of the last known state.

title: Migrating live traffic to a CORS configuration using an overly permissive wildcard with credentials with shadow execution
spec: Describe how to compare output between legacy systems and a CORS configuration using an overly permissive wildcard with credentials using dark launches or traffic mirroring. Malicious third-party websites initiate cross-origin credentialed requests to sensitive intranet APIs. Success: names the comparison metric and how differences are reconciled without affecting users.
result: The primary comparison metric is the **responsepayload hash (e.g., SHA256) per endpoint** generated from the legacy system and from the CORSenabled service under the same request. By mirroring live traffic to a shadow instance that uses the permissive "*" wildcard withAccessControlAllowCredentials, you capture both hashes and log any mismatches. When a hash difference is detected, the system automatically routes the offending request to the legacy backend while flagging the discrepancy for offline analysis, ensuring no user sees an error. After the root cause is fixed, the shadow route is removed and the wildcard configuration is tightened.

title: Putting a load test run against a staging environment under change control
spec: Define the review and approval gate that a load test run against a staging environment must pass before it is altered in a shared environment. The results look fine but production has different hardware, so the capacity estimate is fiction. Success: names one change that should be rejected and the check that catches it.
result: The review gate must reject any load test run where the estimated capacity exceeds the actual measured throughput of the specific staging hardware configuration because production environments often utilize distinct server classes or storage arrays that invalidate cross-environment extrapolations. The critical check that catches this rejection is a direct comparison between the simulated request volume and the observed latency spikes under sustained load on the exact physical nodes used in the staging cluster, which reveals when theoretical models fail to account for real-world resource constraints leading to production capacity fiction.

title: Quantifying the impact of probabilistic Bloom filter cache invalidation on read latency in a multitenant inmemory store
spec: Provide a brief description of a Bloom filter based invalidation scheme where each tenant's keys are hashed into a shared filter with a configurable falsepositive rate. Model the expected additional read latency introduced by false positives given N tenants, average key access rate , filter size M bits, and k hash functions. Derive a formula for the expected extra latency per read assuming a cache miss incurs a 200s backend fetch and a cache hit 2s. Validate the model with a small simulation (e.g., 10,000 operations) and report the observed vs. predicted latency increase. Success: A closedform expression for extra latency and simulation results that match the prediction within 5%.
result: To quantify the impact of probabilistic Bloom filter cache invalidation on read latency, we propose a shared Bloom filter-based invalidation scheme with a configurable false positive rate. The expected additional read latency introduced by false positives can be modeled using the following formula:  ΔL = (1 - (1 - p)^k) * (1 - (1 - (1 - p)^k)^N) * (200 - 2) / (1 - (1 - p)^k)^N  where ΔL is the expected extra latency per read, p is the false positive rate, k is the number of hash functions, N is the number of tenants, and M is the filter size (not explicitly used in the formula, but can be used to estimate p). title: Mapping the dependency chain of nohup without redirecting stdin
spec: Enumerate what nohup without redirecting stdin depends on and what depends on it, and which single dependency kills the whole chain when it fails. The process inherits the terminal and blocks or dies on the first read. Success: names the critical dependency and one way to verify it is healthy.
result: The critical dependency for `nohup` without redirecting stdin is the terminal's ability to provide input without blocking indefinitely. When stdin is not redirected, `nohup` inherits the terminal, and on the first `read()`, the process blocks or dies because the terminal is not a regular file and may be in a state where it cannot supply EOF or data. The dependency chain is: terminal device → stdin file descriptor → `nohup` process. One way to verify the terminal is healthy is to run `test -t 0` which checks if file descriptor 0 (stdin) is open on a terminal; this will return success (0) if it is a valid terminal, and failure otherwise.

title: Scheduling maintenance windows for json.load on untrusted input
spec: Work out when json.load on untrusted input can be taken down safely, how to announce it, and what to do when the window overlaps a traffic peak. Depth and size are the limits worth setting, not the schema. Success: names one task that needs a full maintenance window and one that can run live.
result: json.load on untrusted input must be taken down safely only during a scheduled maintenance window when no production system depends on it. Announce via a change advisory board, email, and status page, giving at least 48 hours notice. If the window overlaps a traffic peak, defer or split it: perform a live schema validation upgrade separately, then take the full parser offline later. A full maintenance window is needed for adding depth and recursion limits to json.load, which breaks existing payloads. A live change—without downtime—is safe for adding size limits, as you can reject oversized payloads in middleware before json.load runs.

title: Proving a database table with no primary key works instead of assuming it
spec: Describe a check that proves a database table with no primary key is doing its job and fails loudly when it is not. Duplicate rows accumulate and every UPDATE touches all the copies, not just one. Success: gives a check with an explicit pass condition and an explicit fail condition.
result: Run a natural-key uniqueness and write-fan-out check: PASS if `SELECT COUNT(*) = COUNT(DISTINCT (a,b)) FROM t` is true and the duplicate-group count `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT a,b FROM t GROUP BY a,b HAVING COUNT(*)>1)` is 0; also PASS only if `UPDATE t SET v=:v WHERE a=:a AND b=:b` reports exactly 1 row affected (Postgres `RETURNING`, SQLite `changes()`). FAIL, and raise a loud exception, if `COUNT(*) > COUNT(DISTINCT (a,b))`, any group has `COUNT(*)>1`, or the update touches 0 or >1 rows—because without a primary key the engine cannot enforce uniqueness, so duplicate copies silently accumulate and every UPDATE writes all of them.

title: Staffing the skills needed to operate a code review that blocks on style only
spec: Identify the knowledge someone must have before they are allowed to touch a code review that blocks on style only in production, and how it is verified. The formatting comments get fixed and the actual logic bug ships to production. Success: names one skill that cannot be learned from a runbook and how it is tested.
result: They must know how to use a linter or formatter tool (e.g., Prettier, ESLint with `--fix`) that automatically resolves style violations. This skill cannot be learned from a runbook because it requires practical judgment to decide when to trust the tool’s automatic output versus manually override a false positive that would delay a fix. Verification: they are given a code sample containing a deliberate simple logic bug alongside a style violation, and must apply the linter, bypass the style-only rule, and merge the logic fix without introducing any new style errors. Passing confirms they can operate review gates effectively.

title: Designing the backup and restore drill for a dashboard built from the same data as the alert
spec: Specify what a restore rehearsal of a dashboard built from the same data as the alert must prove, including the recovery time target and the data-loss boundary. Both go blind together when ingestion breaks. Success: names one backup artifact worth restoring periodically and one assumption the drill exposes.
result: The restore rehearsal must prove that the dashboard can be rebuilt from cold backup artifacts within a recovery time target of four hours, and that the maximum data loss boundary is five minutes from the last successful recovery point. Because ingestion and the alert share the same pipeline, the drill tests end-to-end recovery from the shared data source. One backup artifact worth restoring periodically is a snapshot of the underlying database used for the dashboard queries. One assumption the drill exposes is that the backup artifact is consistent with the alert’s state at the time of the last ingestion checkpoint.

title: Attack surface of an SLO with no error budget policy
spec: Map what an untrusted party can influence in an SLO with no error budget policy and what that influence buys them. The team tracks the SLO but has no rule for when to stop shipping risky changes. Success: names one input worth distrusting and the check that contains it.
result: An untrusted party can influence the SLI (service level indicator) by artificially generating errors or traffic patterns that degrade the metric. For example, they can send malformed requests that cause 5xx errors, lowering the SLI. Without an error budget policy, there is no enforced pause on deployments, so this manipulation allows them to continue degrading service quality while the team still ships risky changes. The input worth distrusting is the HTTP status code returned by the service. The check that contains it is the SLI calculation that counts 5xx responses as failures, dividing them by total requests.

title: Staffing the skills needed to operate a log file nobody rotates
spec: Identify the knowledge someone must have before they are allowed to touch a log file nobody rotates in production, and how it is verified. It fills the partition and takes unrelated services down with it. Success: names one skill that cannot be learned from a runbook and how it is tested.
result: The single required skill is deep understanding of system state correlation which cannot be learned from a runbook because it requires synthesizing temporal patterns across unrelated service dependencies to predict cascading failures before they occur, and this skill is tested by presenting the candidate with a synthetic scenario containing three distinct log streams where two services are intentionally misconfigured to cause a third service to enter an unrecoverable state within ninety seconds, requiring the candidate to identify the root cause without access to external documentation or historical runbooks.

title: Changing an API versioned only by URL path once something depends on it
spec: Describe what makes an API versioned only by URL path hard to change after other things rely on it, and the order of steps that keeps both versions working meanwhile. A breaking change ships under the same path and old clients fail without knowing why. Success: names one step that must come before the switch and one thing that has to keep answering during it.
result: URL path-based versioning (e.g., `/v1/resource`) makes change hard because the version is embedded in every request path. Once clients depend on version X, you cannot alter its behavior without breaking those clients. The safe migration order is: first, deploy the new version code at a new path (e.g., `/v2/resource`) alongside the old one. Before any switch, you must update all clients to call the new path. Then, you can redirect or decommission the old endpoint. During the switch, the one thing that must keep answering is the old version’s endpoint at its original path, so un-migrated clients still succeed.

title: Recovering after a proxy with no upstream timeout has already gone wrong
spec: Lay out the recovery path once a proxy with no upstream timeout has misbehaved and state is inconsistent. A hung upstream holds the connection open forever and the proxy's thread pool drains. Success: gives one ordered recovery step and names something that must not be retried blindly.
result: First, terminate the hung upstream connection from the proxy side by force-closing the socket and clearing the proxy's connection pool for that upstream. This frees the stuck thread and prevents further threads from being consumed by the same upstream. Do not blindly retry the same upstream request with the same parameters — doing so will immediately re-enter the hang condition, draining the thread pool again. Instead, apply a circuit breaker to block new requests to that upstream for a configured cooldown period, then re-route traffic to a healthy replica or fallback endpoint to allow state reconciliation.

title: Testing a config value overridden in three places without a full environment
spec: Work out how to exercise a config value overridden in three places when the real dependencies are not available, and which part of the behaviour a stub can never cover. Nobody can tell which override wins, so the effective value is discovered only by testing. Success: names one thing worth faking and one thing that must be tested for real.
result: To exercise a config value overridden in three places without a full environment, fake the config loader or file system that reads the override sources (e.g., environment variables, local config files, remote config service). This lets you inject known values and test precedence logic without real dependencies. A stub can never cover the external override source’s actual behavior—such as latency, parsing errors, or authentication failures when fetching from a remote config server. That must be tested for real, because stubs bypass the runtime conditions that can produce unexpected fallback or crash states.

title: Multi-region failover and split-brain recovery for TLS termination at the edge
spec: Define how TLS termination at the edge routes traffic and reconciles diverging state when an entire cloud region drops off. Traffic behind the edge is plaintext, which is a decision, not an accident. Success: specifies the quorum rule or conflict resolution algorithm used.
result: The system implements a weighted majority quorum rule where TLS termination at the edge routes traffic based on active leader elections that require two-thirds of available regional nodes to agree before any state divergence triggers a split-brain recovery protocol, ensuring that when an entire cloud region drops off the remaining healthy regions continue serving encrypted traffic while automatically reconciling diverging session states by rolling back to the last known consistent ledger entry stored in the central consensus store if the quorum threshold is not met within thirty seconds of detection.

title: Chain replication: linearizable reads and writes from a line of replicas rather than a quorum or a primary
spec: You want to replicate data across several nodes for fault tolerance while keeping strong, linearizable consistency and good throughput. Primary-backup makes one primary serve every read and write and fan each write out to the backups, so the primary is a bottleneck and reads contend with writes. Quorum systems make every read and write touch an overlapping subset and reason carefully about those overlaps. Chain replication takes a third shape. Arrange the replicas in a line: a head, some middle nodes, and a tail. A write enters at the head, which applies it and forwards it down the chain node by node, each node applying then forwarding, and only when the write reaches the tail and the tail applies it does the tail acknowledge the client. So a write is committed exactly when the tail has it, and because it walked through every node in the same order, all replicas apply writes in one identical order and every committed write sits on every node. Reads are served entirely by the tail. The tail holds only committed state, since a value arrives there only after passing through the whole chain, so a single read at the tail returns the latest committed value and is linearizable, with no quorum and no multi-node read. The work splits cleanly: the head admits writes, interior nodes just relay and apply, and the tail serves all reads and sends all acknowledgements. A coordinator monitors the chain and handles failures. If the head dies its successor becomes the new head; if the tail dies its predecessor becomes the new tail, and it already holds every write the old tail had; if a middle node dies it is spliced out by joining its predecessor to its successor and resending any writes it had not yet forwarded. Managing these membership changes safely is the subtle part, and the coordinator is itself usually replicated by a consensus protocol. The tradeoff against primary-backup and quorums is that you get strong consistency with single-node reads and dead-simple ordering with no quorum arithmetic, but write latency is the full traversal of the chain and the tail alone bounds read throughput. That last limit is what CRAQ, chain replication with apportioned queries, removes: let any node answer reads, with each node marking an object clean or dirty, answering locally when clean and asking the tail only for the committed version when a write is in flight, which spreads reads across all nodes while staying linearizable. The deeper idea is that instead of a star, where a primary talks to all backups, or a quorum, where everyone talks to a subset, you lay the replicas in a line so that order is enforced by the topology itself: writes are totally ordered by walking from head to tail, and the tail, being last, holds exactly the committed prefix, so one read there is strongly consistent. You get linearizability from the shape of the network rather than from voting.
